finding.title: vanilla_ppo checkpoint save is not atomic, and the resume scan's catch-all turns a torn newest checkpoint into a silent full-progress wipe
finding.failure_scenario: trainer.py:7391 writes the every-10-iter checkpoint with a bare `torch.save(_ckpt_payload, str(ckpt_path))` — no tmp+rename, unlike the GA path (checkpointing.py:56 save_checkpoint_atomic) and save_winner (checkpointing.py:370-381), which both do tmp+fsync+os.replace. Kill during the save (OOM kill, SIGKILL, or Ctrl-C — KeyboardInterrupt is NOT caught by the `except Exception` at 7393 and train_game.py:670 treats it as a clean stop) leaves a truncated vanilla_ppo_iter_00510.pt as the highest-numbered file. On the next launch/supervisor relaunch, _maybe_resume_vanilla_ppo picks it (trainer.py:4236-4241, highest iter number), torch.load raises, and the catch-all at 4273-4278 logs 'auto-resume scan failed (starting fresh)' and returns iter_offset=0: the run silently restarts from RANDOM weights while ~50 good checkpoints sit on disk — and, because fresh_start=False, _load_smb_curriculum_from_disk still resumes the curriculum at stage N, so a random net trains from deep-rung warm starts. Worse, iter numbering restarts at 0, so new saves overwrite the old run's good iter_00010/00020/... files (the exact destroy-good-run failure the comment at 4484-4490 documents), and every subsequent crash re-picks the torn 00510 until numbering passes it. Under the 14010eb supervisor this happens unattended overnight: one mid-save death converts a 500-iter run into from-scratch training with no crash, only a WARNING line.
finding.fix_sketch: 1) Make the save atomic: torch.save to ckpt_path.with_suffix('.pt.tmp'), fsync (reuse checkpointing._fsync_best_effort), then os.replace — same dance save_winner already does. 2) Make resume tear-tolerant: iterate the sorted candidates newest→oldest, wrapping only torch.load per candidate; on load failure, log loudly and try the next-older checkpoint (optionally rename the corrupt file to *.corrupt so it stops winning the sort) instead of falling back to random weights. 3) Only start fresh when zero candidates load, and log that at ERROR, not WARNING.

verdict.reasons: Every link in the claimed failure path checks out in the code. (1) trainer.py:7391 is a bare torch.save to the final path — no tmp/fsync/os.replace — while the GA path (checkpointing.py save_checkpoint_atomic, :56-91) and save_winner (:370-381) both do the atomic dance, so this is the one writer that skipped the established pattern. (2) A mid-save death genuinely leaves a torn highest-numbered file: the except Exception at 7393 does not catch KeyboardInterrupt, and scripts/train_game.py:670-672 treats Ctrl-C as a clean stop (return 0, no relaunch); SIGKILL/OOM need no handler. Aggravator: the save builds a full CPU copy of net+optimizer+RND state (7361-7376), so OOM kills are correlated with the vulnerable window. (3) _maybe_resume_vanilla_ppo (4236-4242) tries ONLY the highest-numbered file; torch.load on a truncated zip raises an Exception subclass, and the catch-all at 4273-4278 logs one WARNING ('starting fresh') and returns iter_offset=0 with no fallback to older candidates — which do sit on disk, since rotate_old_checkpoints only globs gen_*.pt (checkpointing.py:156), so vanilla_ppo_iter_*.pt accumulate (~50 for a 500-iter run). _vppo_resumed_from_iter stays None so the GUI resume banner (4498-4506) is absent — silent as claimed. (4) train_game.py:667 makes every supervisor relaunch fresh_start=False, so _load_smb_curriculum_from_disk (4310-4316) still warm-starts the random net at stage N. (5) global_it = it + iter_offset (5263), so the restarted run overwrites the old run's iter_00010/00020/... — the exact destroy-good-run failure the comment at 4484-4490 documents as having happened before — and the torn file stays highest-numbered, so each further crash repeats the wipe until numbering passes it. (6) 14010eb (HEAD) is real; its unattended-relaunch supervisor makes the overnight scenario concrete, and its poison-save guard (7338-7354) checks NaN params, not file integrity, so it does not cover this. Severity corrected critical→high: the trigger requires a process death landing inside a save window of roughly seconds per 10 iterations (real but probabilistic, though OOM-correlated), winners/best.pt survives untouched, and older good checkpoints remain recoverable until the fresh run progressively overwrites them — serious silent data loss under a plausible trigger rather than a deterministic common-path failure. The proposed fix (atomic tmp+os.replace, newest-to-oldest load fallback with per-candidate try, quarantine/rename of corrupt files, ERROR-level log only when zero candidates load) is the correct shape and reuses existing helpers.

finding.title: Supervisor relaunch of a crashed --no-resume run silently resumes the PREVIOUS run's checkpoints and curriculum stage
finding.failure_scenario: train_game.py:667 passes `fresh_start=(not args.resume) and attempt == 0`, so only attempt 0 of a `--no-resume` run is fresh; any crash relaunch runs with fresh_start=False. But a fresh start deliberately leaves the prior run's files in place: trainer.py:4220-4232 skips-but-keeps old vanilla_ppo_iter_*.pt, and trainer.py:4310-4330 skips-but-keeps smb_curriculum/stage_NN.state. The fresh run also restarts iter numbering at 0, so its own checkpoints (iter_00010...) are always numbered BELOW the abandoned run's (e.g. iter_02040). When the fresh run crashes at any point — even after saving its own checkpoints — the relaunch's resume scan (trainer.py:4236-4241) picks the OLD run's iter_02040.pt by highest number, and _load_smb_curriculum_from_disk(fresh_start=False) resumes the OLD run's stage-5 curriculum. The explicitly-requested from-scratch experiment silently morphs mid-flight into a resume of the run the user told it to ignore, discarding the fresh run's progress AND contaminating its metrics/claims — the exact 'fresh run resumed at stage 2' validated confusion, now automated by the self-healing supervisor with only log lines to notice.
finding.fix_sketch: On fresh_start, epoch-fence the directory: write a `fresh_epoch.json` marker with the run's start timestamp (or archive prior vanilla_ppo_iter_*.pt + smb_curriculum/ into runs/<ts>/, mirroring archive_previous_run), and make _maybe_resume_vanilla_ppo and _load_smb_curriculum_from_disk ignore any file with mtime older than the marker. Then the supervisor's fresh_start-only-on-attempt-0 logic becomes safe: relaunches resume only checkpoints the crashed fresh run itself wrote.

verdict.reasons: Every link in the claimed path is real. train_game.py:667 passes fresh_start=(not args.resume) and attempt == 0 with a default restart budget of 5 (line 660), so only attempt 0 of a --no-resume run is fresh. A fresh start deliberately keeps prior files: trainer.py:4220-4232 skips-but-keeps old vanilla_ppo_iter_*.pt and returns iter_offset=0, and trainer.py:4310-4330 skips-but-keeps smb_curriculum/stage_NN.state ("NEVER deleted or moved"). The fresh run numbers its checkpoints from global_it = it + 0 (trainer.py:5263, saved at 7355-7358), so they are always numerically below an abandoned longer run's. On any crash, the relaunch (fresh_start=False) resume scan at trainer.py:4236-4241 sorts by the integer filename suffix — not mtime — and loads the OLD run's highest-numbered checkpoint (net + optimizer + RND + gx_counts + anticollapse + iter offset), and _load_smb_curriculum_from_disk (called with fresh_start=False at 4653) inherits the OLD run's curriculum stages. No guard exists elsewhere: archive_previous_run (checkpointing.py:192-250) moves only metrics.jsonl and copies gen_*.pt; rotate_old_checkpoints globs only gen_*.pt; there is no epoch marker or mtime fence anywhere on the vanilla_ppo resume path; derive_checkpoint_dir (profile_utils.py:56-75) is a stable per-game dir shared across runs. Ironically, rotate_old_checkpoints' docstring (checkpointing.py:140-143) documents this exact restart-counters-at-0 hazard and sorts by mtime for the GA path, while the vanilla_ppo scan does not. Severity stays high: the failure is automated by the default-on supervisor, silently violates an explicit --no-resume request, and this repo has documented precedent of silent-resume confusion invalidating experiments (comments at trainer.py:4295-4297, 4499-4501). It is not critical because the resume IS surfaced (log line at 4267-4272 plus resumed_from_iter on every metrics emission at 4503-4506), no irreplaceable data is destroyed, and detection post-hoc is possible — though minor collateral exists (the fresh run overwrites the old run's same-named low-numbered checkpoint files).

finding.title: RND state is never restored on vanilla_ppo resume: RND is built (and pending state applied as a no-op) BEFORE _maybe_resume_vanilla_ppo stashes it
finding.failure_scenario: In _run_vanilla_ppo, the RND module is eagerly built at trainer.py:4464-4471 and `_apply_pending_rnd_state()` runs at 4479 — at which point `self._pending_rnd_state` is still None (init at line 846), so it returns without doing anything. Only afterwards does _maybe_resume_vanilla_ppo (called at 4494) stash the checkpoint's rnd_state_dict into _pending_rnd_state (4256). It is then never applied: the only other apply site (3888) is inside _reinforce_update (GA path, not used by vanilla_ppo), and the rebuild guard `self._rnd is None` at 4464 ensures no second build ever happens. Net effect: every resume — including every 14010eb supervisor relaunch — silently resets the RND predictor weights AND the obs/reward running-normalization stats, while the checkpoint dutifully carries them (payload written at 7372-7376 'so resume keeps the novelty memory'). Post-resume, the entire already-explored corridor is re-scored as novel and the intrinsic-reward normalizer re-warms from scratch, pulling the policy back toward trodden ground for hundreds of iters — a silent regression after each crash, in the same dead-state class as sticky_action_prob (parsed-but-dead) and _load_worker_state.
finding.fix_sketch: Call `self._apply_pending_rnd_state()` immediately after the `iter_offset = self._maybe_resume_vanilla_ppo(...)` call at 4494 (the module already exists by then, so the lazy-build rationale in the 7489 docstring no longer applies to this path). Alternatively move the RND build block below the resume call. Add an assertion/log when _pending_rnd_state is non-None at loop start to catch future reorderings.

verdict.reasons: Traced end-to-end in src/training/trainer.py and every structural claim holds. (1) _run_vanilla_ppo builds RND eagerly at 4464-4471 and calls _apply_pending_rnd_state() at 4479, when _pending_rnd_state is still None (init at 846) — the guard at 7493 makes it a no-op. (2) _maybe_resume_vanilla_ppo (called at 4494, after the build) stashes the checkpoint's rnd_state_dict at 4256 under a stale comment claiming RND "builds lazily ... after this resume block" — true only for the GA path. (3) The stash is then dead: the file's only other apply site (3888) is inside _reinforce_update (GA path, called solely at 2532), and the `self._rnd is None` guard at 4464 plus the absence of any other `self._rnd =` assignment means no later build/apply ever occurs in the vanilla loop. (4) The save side works (7372-7376 persists rnd_state_dict "so resume keeps the novelty memory"), so the restore is silently dead and the "restored RND state" log at 7497 can never fire on this path. Compounding: optimizer.load_state_dict at 4246 restores Adam moments for RND predictor params onto freshly-random weights. Exposure is real: active campaign configs enable RND (smb_oneshot_tiles 0.1, smb_consolidate_level_tiles 0.1, smb_1_4_go_explore 0.1, several games 0.5) and the workflow is resume-heavy (supervisor relaunch, Run B resume). Severity high stands: deterministic on every RND-enabled resume, silent, defeats a purpose-built checkpoint feature, in the project's known experiment-invalidating dead-state class — though not a crash and self-heals as the predictor re-warms. Only overstatement: "hundreds of iters" of policy regression is a magnitude estimate, not code-provable; the provable effect is full reset of predictor + target + normalization stats.

finding.title: save_winner compares metric_value across DIFFERENT metric_names: an old inflated clear_rate winner permanently blocks the ladder-mode cold_seq_clear_rate champion
finding.failure_scenario: save_winner's overwrite gate (checkpointing.py:350-357) compares the incoming metric_value against prev['metric_value'] without ever checking prev['metric_name']. The trainer writes under two different metrics depending on mode: 'clear_rate' (training telemetry) in plain mode (trainer.py:7423-7430) and 'cold_seq_clear_rate' (the DoD number) in ladder mode (trainer.py:7412-7421). Concrete case: winners/best.json in the SMB dir holds clear_rate=0.88 from a pre-07-16 run — a number the campaign log says is die-respawn/telemetry inflated. The ladder campaign then achieves a genuine cold sequential clear rate of 0.6; save_winner computes 0.6 < 0.88 and returns False on every save, forever. Since find_playable_checkpoint (checkpointing.py:524-527) prefers winners/best.pt unconditionally, `make demo`/`make eval` keep playing the stale policy and the true cold champion is never pinned anywhere on disk (best_cold_snapshot lives only in process memory) — defeating the exact §Q2 rule that training telemetry must never select the deliverable.
finding.fix_sketch: In save_winner, when prev is present but prev.get('metric_name') != metric_name, treat the slot as having no comparable best: either overwrite (logging the metric change loudly) or, cleaner, key winners per metric (winners/best_<metric_name>.pt + sidecar) and teach find_playable_checkpoint a preference order (cold_seq_clear_rate > clear_rate). Also have ladder mode persist best_cold_snapshot in the iter checkpoint payload so the cold champion survives a crash between winner saves.

verdict.reasons: Mechanism CONFIRMED in code: save_winner (checkpointing.py:350-357) compares metric_value against prev['metric_value'] without ever checking prev['metric_name'], and trainer.py:7412-7430 writes the same winners/ slot under 'cold_seq_clear_rate' (ladder) vs 'clear_rate' (plain, from vppo_success_rate telemetry) into the same out_dir. find_playable_checkpoint (checkpointing.py:524-527) prefers winners/best.pt unconditionally and is the live path for scripts/demo_game.py:79 and scripts/eval_game.py:190. However the scenario is overstated on three counts. (1) The concrete instance is constructed, not observed: I read every winners/best.json on disk — the two ladder-mode dirs (super_mario_bros_one_shot, super_mario_bros_one_shot_tiles) hold cold_seq_clear_rate=0.0 sidecars and have never contained a clear_rate winner, so nothing is being blocked today. The collision requires the SAME checkpoint dir to transition modes: ladder_on comes from the profile YAML (reinforce.substage_ladder.enabled, trainer.py:4695-4698) while the dir is derived from the profile name (profile_utils.py:56-75), and the campaign's practice has been new profile names per mode (_v2, _runB, one_shot_tiles). It is a realistic future config edit — super_mario_bros_tiles_vanilla/winners/best.json genuinely holds a pre-07-16 telemetry clear_rate=0.69 that would block a ladder run reusing that profile — but the trigger precondition has never fired. (2) The claim that the cold champion 'lives only in process memory' is factually wrong: trainer.py:6535-6544 persists best_cold.pt (with metric name/value) to checkpoint_dir at probe time on every strict improvement, so it survives crashes; the true residual gap is only that find_playable_checkpoint does not know about best_cold.pt. (3) The finding misses the symmetric, equally-real direction: ladder→plain transition lets inflated telemetry clear_rate silently OVERWRITE an honest cold champion — same root cause. The fix sketch (refuse cross-metric comparison / key winners per metric, teach find_playable_checkpoint a preference order) is sound; the consolidate_on branch (trainer.py:7405-7411) shows the authors already guard this hazard elsewhere. Real latent bug on the deliverable-selection path, silent when it fires, but precondition-gated, unmanifested, and with a disk-recoverable champion — severity low, not medium.

finding.title: run_manifest.json is unconditionally overwritten on every (re)launch, destroying the provenance (seed/git commit/hyperparams) of the run it is supposed to make citable
finding.failure_scenario: write_run_manifest is called on every train_game.py invocation before the supervisor loop (train_game.py:624-641), and run_manifest.py:79-83 unconditionally replaces <checkpoint_dir>/run_manifest.json. A resumed run therefore rewrites the manifest with the CURRENT git commit, seed, created_at, and pinned hyperparams. Concrete case: Run B trained 600 iters at commit X with seed 7; overnight crash; morning resume happens after pulling fix 935e609 (new commit, possibly new profile hyperparams, different/default seed). The manifest now claims the entire 600+ iter run — including all checkpoints and metrics.jsonl rows already written — was produced at the new commit/seed/config. Every receipt that cites the manifest (the CLAIMS.md ledger, scoreboard provenance joins, 'which commit trained these weights' debugging) is silently wrong for the majority of the run, and the original values are unrecoverable. This is the same integrity class as the eval --start-state dead knob: the artifact exists and looks authoritative but no longer describes what actually happened.
finding.fix_sketch: In train_game.py, only call write_run_manifest when the run is fresh (fresh_start) or the file doesn't exist. For resumes, append instead of replace: add a 'resumes' list entry ({git_commit, seed, created_at, resumed_from_iter}) to the existing manifest (or drop timestamped sidecars in run_manifest.d/). Keep the original top-level fields immutable, and have write_run_manifest refuse to change rom_md5/seed silently — log at ERROR if they differ from the recorded values.

verdict.reasons: Traced end-to-end and every claim holds. (1) train_game.py:624-641 calls write_run_manifest unconditionally on every invocation before the supervisor loop, regardless of --resume. (2) run_manifest.py:79-83 bare-replaces <checkpoint_dir>/run_manifest.json with no existence check or merge. (3) derive_checkpoint_dir (profile_utils.py:56-75) returns a stable per-game path (checkpoints/<slug>), so a resume writes over the original run's manifest. (4) Field corruption is exactly as claimed: git_commit re-derived at write time (run_manifest.py:70), created_at re-stamped (line 71, launcher doesn't pass it), seed comes from the current invocation with argparse default 0 (train_game.py:517) so an un-repeated seed flag silently records 0, and pinned hyperparams are re-read from the possibly-edited profile (line 77). (5) Unrecoverable: no other artifact records commit/seed — checkpoint payloads (trainer.py:7361-7391) hold iter+state dicts only, launcher log omits seed/commit; only resumed_from_iter on metrics rows survives. (6) The receipts leg is real: scripts/scoreboard.py:103,153 reads the manifest for its provenance section, and docs/proposals/smb_oneshot_campaign.md:513 cites checkpoints/mario_2_1_runB/run_manifest.json — the exact Run B staged for morning resume after commit 935e609, so the scenario is the project's literal next action, not hypothetical. Aggravating fact the finding missed: a second unconditional caller inside Trainer._run_vanilla_ppo (trainer.py:4512-4526, no fresh_start gate) means GUI-driven runs overwrite too, and a launcher-only fix would not close the bug — the guard must live in/below write_run_manifest. Severity medium is calibrated: silent corruption of an authoritative provenance artifact (high value in this receipts-focused project) but no impact on training behavior, checkpoints, or results — only their attributability.

finding.title: Vanilla-PPO checkpoints and campaign deliverables are written non-atomically; a kill mid-save poisons auto-resume
finding.failure_scenario: trainer.py:7391 writes vanilla_ppo_iter_NNNNN.pt with a raw torch.save to the final path — no tmp+rename, unlike the GA path's save_checkpoint_atomic (checkpointing.py:56-91). The same raw pattern writes best_cold.pt (trainer.py:6536) and the consolidation deliverable best_<level>.pt (trainer.py:6729, 6772) — the latter is also the rollback target the gate's 'regress' action reloads. The payload (net + optimizer + RND + anticollapse snapshot) is tens-to-hundreds of MB, so the write window is real. Concrete triggers, all in the current workflow: (a) Ctrl-C on a foreground `make train` — KeyboardInterrupt can land inside torch.save; train_game.py:670 then reports 'clean stop' and leaves the truncated file; (b) `kill <pid>` on a nohup run — no SIGTERM handler exists anywhere in train_game.py/trainer.py, so default TERM aborts mid-write with no finally/teardown; (c) closing the GUI — the training thread is daemon=True (gui/main.py:410) and gets frozen at interpreter exit mid-write after the 3 s join at gui/main.py:863; (d) OOM/MPS-driver kill during an overnight run. Additionally the except at trainer.py:7393-7394 catches an in-process write failure (disk full) but never unlinks the partial file. In every case the truncated file is the HIGHEST-numbered checkpoint, i.e. exactly the one auto-resume selects — see the next finding for how that silently destroys the run. This directly defeats the 1-day-old poison-save guard (trainer.py:7338-7354), which checks parameter finiteness but not write integrity.
finding.fix_sketch: Route all four write sites through the existing atomic pattern: torch.save to path.with_suffix('.pt.tmp'), flush+os.fsync, os.replace to final (reuse/extract the helper from checkpointing.py:56). In the except branch, unlink the tmp file. Optionally install a SIGTERM handler in train_game.main() that raises KeyboardInterrupt so nohup kills get the same graceful path as Ctrl-C.

verdict.reasons: Every load-bearing claim verified in code. (1) trainer.py:7391 is a raw torch.save to the final vanilla_ppo_iter_NNNNN.pt path — no tmp/fsync/os.replace — while the GA path's save_checkpoint_atomic (checkpointing.py:56-91) does the full atomic dance; the vanilla path never calls it. (2) The same raw pattern writes best_cold.pt (trainer.py:6536) and best_<level>.pt (6729, 6772, plus a fourth site the finding missed at 5030). (3) The except at 7393-7394 only logs and never unlinks a partial file. (4) No SIGTERM handler exists anywhere (grep confirms; only os.setpgrp at 7609, which propagates kills tree-wide), the supervisor's KeyboardInterrupt handler (train_game.py ~670) reports 'clean stop' leaving the truncated file, and the GUI training thread is daemon=True (gui/main.py ~410) with a 3s join (~862) so interpreter exit can freeze it mid-save. (5) Impact chain confirmed and slightly WORSE than stated: _maybe_resume_vanilla_ppo (trainer.py:4236-4277) loads only the single highest-numbered checkpoint, and a truncated zip's torch.load exception is swallowed by a broad except that logs a warning and starts the run FRESH from random weights — no fallback to the second-newest checkpoint, so the crash supervisor's assumption that a bad checkpoint 'crashes on load' never triggers. The finiteness guard (7338-7354) checks values, not write integrity. One minor misstatement: the gate's rollback action (6706) reloads the in-memory accepted_snapshot, not the best_<level>.pt file — the file is the deliverable consumed downstream, not the in-run rollback source; this does not change the conclusion. Severity corrected critical→high: the mechanism is real and the consequence severe (silent full-run restart in a kill/resume-heavy workflow), but it fires only when a kill lands inside the save window (roughly ~1% of wall time — a sub-second-to-few-second write once every 10 iters), and older intact checkpoints remain on disk for manual recovery, so it is not a deterministic loss on every interrupt.

finding.title: Vanilla resume treats ANY load failure as 'start fresh' — a single corrupt newest checkpoint silently discards the whole run and overwrites surviving good checkpoints
finding.failure_scenario: _maybe_resume_vanilla_ppo (trainer.py:4236-4242) sorts vanilla_ppo_iter_*.pt by iter number and torch.loads ONLY the newest; the entire scan+load is wrapped in `except Exception: log.warning('auto-resume scan failed (starting fresh)')` at 4273-4277, returning iter_offset 0. Scenario: overnight run at iter 580 is killed mid-save (previous finding), leaving a truncated iter-580 file while iters 10..570 are intact on disk (vanilla files are never rotated — rotate_old_checkpoints only globs gen_*.pt, checkpointing.py:156). The train_game.py supervisor (or the next `make train`, resume defaulting on at train_game.py:504) relaunches: torch.load raises, the warning scrolls past in nohup.out, and training restarts from RANDOM weights with checkpoint numbering restarted at 0 — so the new run's iter-10, iter-20... saves progressively OVERWRITE the old good checkpoints at the same filenames, while the corrupt iter-580 file keeps shadowing every future resume attempt. The supervisor sees no crash, so its 'a checkpoint that crashes on load needs a human' design intent (train_game.py:655-657) never engages. Days of training are destroyed with only a single WARNING line as evidence — same silent-integrity class as the dead --start-state and title-screen-demo incidents.
finding.fix_sketch: Iterate candidates newest→oldest and fall back to the next-older checkpoint on load failure (log loudly, and rename the corrupt file to *.corrupt so it stops shadowing). If checkpoints exist but none load, raise instead of returning 0 — that converts silent destruction into the supervisor's intended fast-fail-for-humans path. Never reuse iter numbering below the highest existing file.

verdict.reasons: Every element of the failure path verifies against the code. (1) trainer.py:4234-4278: _maybe_resume_vanilla_ppo sorts vanilla_ppo_iter_*.pt by iter number, torch.loads ONLY the newest, and wraps the whole scan+load in `except Exception` that logs one WARNING and returns iter_offset 0 — no fallback to older intact checkpoints, no quarantine of the corrupt file, no raise. (2) The trigger is real: the iter-checkpoint save at trainer.py:7391 is a bare torch.save to the final path — NOT atomic, unlike winners/best.pt which uses tmp+fsync+os.replace (checkpointing.py:370-381), so a SIGKILL/OOM/power-loss mid-save leaves a truncated file at the winning filename; even Ctrl-C works since KeyboardInterrupt is a BaseException and escapes the `except Exception` at 7393. (3) rotate_old_checkpoints (checkpointing.py:156) globs only gen_*.pt, so older good vanilla checkpoints survive as untried fallbacks while the corrupt newest file shadows every future resume forever. (4) scripts/train_game.py:504 defaults --resume on, and the supervisor comment at 651-657 confirms the 'crash-on-load needs a human' intent that the swallowed exception bypasses — the supervisor sees a normal run. (5) The overwrite consequence is even self-documented: trainer.py:4484-4490 admits that iter_offset=0 'rewrites vanilla_ppo_iter_00010.pt, _00020.pt, …' and 'is how a collapsed resume silently destroyed a good run's checkpoints' — that fix depends entirely on the load succeeding, so a corrupt newest file resurrects the exact documented destruction mode. Severity corrected critical→high: the scenario genuinely fires and silently destroys resumable training state, but (a) the trigger requires an interruption landing inside a ~1s save window every 10 iters (probabilistic, not deterministic), and (b) winners/best.pt — saved atomically, rotation-exempt, overwritten only by a strictly better metric — preserves the best-ever deployable policy through the wipeout, so the flagship artifact survives even though optimizer/RND/gx_counts state and the checkpoint history are lost. The fix sketch (newest→oldest fallback, rename corrupt file to *.corrupt, raise when checkpoints exist but none load, never renumber below the highest existing file) is sound.

finding.title: No run-lock on the checkpoint dir: supervisor backoff window and double nohup launches put two trainers on one dir, corrupting checkpoints and metrics with no kill involved
finding.failure_scenario: There is no pidfile/lock anywhere (verified: no flock/fcntl/O_EXCL in train_game.py, trainer.py, checkpointing.py, run_manifest.py). The supervisor loop (train_game.py:662-694) sleeps 60 s after a fast crash, then relaunches unconditionally. Concrete sequence: a nohup'd run crashes on a poisoned config; the user sees the traceback in nohup.out, fixes it, and starts a new `make train GAME=mario` — 40 s later the OLD supervisor wakes from its backoff and calls trainer.run() again. Now two processes share checkpoints/mario/: the second run() archives-and-truncates the first's live metrics.jsonl and run.log mid-write (trainer.py:1376-1383); both processes torch.save to the SAME vanilla_ppo_iter_NNNNN.pt paths non-atomically, interleaving writes into a corrupt file even though nobody was killed; both auto-resume from each other's checkpoints on their next restart; and 2×24 rayon workers plus two MPS training loops thrash the M4. The same hazard fires on a plain accidental double `nohup make train` — the second launch gives no error at all.
finding.fix_sketch: Acquire an exclusive run lock at Trainer.run() entry (or train_game.main): open(checkpoint_dir/'run.pid', O_CREAT|O_EXCL) writing the pid; on EEXIST, read the pid and probe os.kill(pid, 0) — stale locks (dead pid) are reclaimed, live ones abort with a clear 'already training in this dir (pid N)' error. Supervisor releases/reacquires around each relaunch so a competing process started during backoff wins cleanly. Remove the lock in the run() finally.

(1) No lock exists: grep for flock/fcntl/O_EXCL/pidfile across scripts/train_game.py, src/training/{trainer,checkpointing,run_manifest,metrics_sink}.py and the Makefile finds nothing; `make train` is a bare python invocation. finding.title: GUI Stop's 5-second deadline nulls the still-alive trainer thread, defeating the double-start guard — second in-process trainer on the same checkpoint dir
finding.failure_scenario: _poll_shutdown (gui/main.py:790-796) gives the trainer thread 5 s to exit after Stop, then calls _finalize_stop() which sets self.training_thread = None (gui/main.py:814) while the thread is STILL RUNNING — the code comment admits it 'should' die on the next step_all. But Trainer.stop() only sets _running=False, and the vanilla loop polls it at iteration boundaries (trainer.py:5261, 5293, 5848) — never inside the K-epoch PPO minibatch update, a cold-probe/eval pass, or a checkpoint save, any of which can exceed 5 s on MPS with large batches. _on_start's guard checks exactly self.training_thread.is_alive() (gui/main.py:297), so once it is None the user can Start again: two Trainer instances in one process, both stepping their own 24-worker pool (double the ~17 GB buffer footprint this code already fought — can OOM the host), and both writing to the SAME derived checkpoint dir (derive_checkpoint_dir keys on game name, trainer.py:190): the new run() truncates the old run's metrics.jsonl, and the old trainer's next 10-iter checkpoint save interleaves with the new one's on identical vanilla_ppo_iter filenames (non-atomic, finding 1) — corrupting the resume chain from inside the GUI with zero kills or crashes.
finding.fix_sketch: Do not null the reference while the thread is alive: move it to a self._zombie_threads list and keep the _on_start guard checking both training_thread and any alive zombie (refuse Start until join succeeds). Additionally make Stop responsive by checking self._running inside the PPO epoch/minibatch loop and before each checkpoint save so the 5 s deadline is rarely hit.

verdict.reasons: Core mechanism verified line-by-line. (1) gui/main.py:790-796: after the 5 s deadline _poll_shutdown calls _finalize_stop(), which nulls self.training_thread (line 814) while the thread is still alive. (2) The _on_start guard (gui/main.py:294-309) keys solely on training_thread/is_alive(), so a subsequent Start builds a second Trainer + pool in-process. (3) Trainer.stop() only sets _running=False (trainer.py:7594-7595); the vanilla loop checks it at 5261/5293/5848 but the K-epoch minibatch update (6066-6158), the 10-iter checkpoint save (7339+), and the entire cold-probe pass (cold_probe.py has zero stop polling) do not — on a probe iteration the post-Stop tail can run for minutes, so exceeding 5 s is realistic. (4) Both trainers share the checkpoint dir (derive_checkpoint_dir keyed on game name, trainer.py:189-193). (5) The memory-doubling/OOM concern is corroborated by the code's own comment in _finalize_stop (gui/main.py:816-819), and gc.collect() cannot free buffers the live zombie thread still references. (6) The new run() archives-then-truncates metrics.jsonl (trainer.py:1375-1376) and the zombie's sink appends per-write to the same path (metrics_sink.py:129), so zombie rows contaminate the NEW run's metrics file. However, three tail claims are overstated, which is why severity is corrected to medium: the old run's metrics are archived (moved), not lost; the zombie writes at most ONE final checkpoint before breaking at 5261, and filename collision on vanilla_ppo_iter_*.pt is essentially unreachable (fresh runs number from 0, resumes number past the latest), so "corrupting the resume chain" via interleaved identical filenames does not hold; and stop delivery is reliable (Stop button is the control queue's only producer, listener polls every 0.25 s), so dual-pool overlap is bounded to the remainder of one iteration (seconds typically, minutes on cold-probe iterations), not sustained dual training. Net: a genuine, silently-triggerable GUI lifecycle bug with bounded contamination (foreign metrics rows, one stray checkpoint, transient RSS spike, stale zombie frames in the new grid) — real, but below the claimed catastrophic impact. The fix sketch (zombie-thread list + guard on any alive zombie, plus _running checks inside the epoch loop, before checkpoint saves, and inside the cold probe) is sound.

finding.title: Go-Explore archive saved with raw pickle.dump and reloaded with warning-only fallback — kill mid-save silently wipes the exploration frontier while stats sidecar keeps claiming cells
finding.failure_scenario: GoExploreArchive.save (go_explore.py:249-258) pickle.dumps self._cells — a dict holding a full emulator state blob (~10s of KB) per cell, easily hundreds of MB after a long run — straight onto archive.pkl with no tmp+rename, then writes the stats sidecar. Worse, if the pkl write died before the sidecar write, the surviving older .stats.json still reports the previous cell counts, actively masking the loss during post-hoc analysis. Same silent-corruption class as the npz buffer-aliasing incident.
finding.fix_sketch: In save(): dump to path.with_suffix('.pkl.tmp'), fsync, os.replace; before replacing, rename the existing archive to archive.pkl.bak so one known-good generation always survives. verdict.reasons: Traced end-to-end and every claim checks out. (1) go_explore.py:249-258: save() opens archive.pkl with open(path,'wb') — truncating it immediately — then pickle.dumps self._cells with no tmp+rename/fsync/backup; the .stats.json sidecar is written after the pkl, so a kill during the dump leaves a corrupt pkl next to a stale sidecar still reporting old cell counts (masking claim holds). finding.title: Pool seed is a dead knob; deterministic multi-seed/multi-episode gate evidence is one trajectory counted N times (CONFIRMED: all gate receipts byte-identical)
finding.failure_scenario: RustPool.__init__ stores `self._seed = seed` (line 98) but start() (lines 151-156) never forwards it to nes_core.Pool — the knob is dead. eval_composite.py:223 passes `seed=seed` believing it seeds the env, and stamps `result["seed"] = seed` (eval_composite.py:251) as a self-describing protocol field. So `--seed 0` vs `--seed 1` and every episode within a run are byte-identical replays. Empirically confirmed: md5 of runs/gate_receipts_seed0/ep000+ep001 and gate_receipts_seed1/ep000+ep001 are ALL 796217a2… (one file, four names), and all five W3 receipts across both seeds are 5a6459430c…. The written go/no-go gate ('clears on BOTH gate seeds, 2/2 episodes each', smb_oneshot_campaign.md 07-19) cited four trials that were one trajectory. finding.title: CompositeController leaks _gx_pad across committed level switches and never resets _gx_confirm on area changes — transition-frame garbage gx can fire a premature one-way handoff

(2) the area-change branch (lines 539-564) returns early without resetting _gx_confirm, so the 2-consecutive-frame guard (lines 577-587) — whose stated purpose is 'a mid-transition gx glitch can't fire it' — can be satisfied by two garbage $006D/$0086 reads straddling a pipe/area transition (the exact 57daa80 garbage-gx class): one-way handoff to the back-half net at the wrong point, disclosed in gx_switches with a nonsense gx value.

finding.title: vanilla_ppo resume has zero checkpoint/profile validation: shape drift silently degrades to fresh start, key drift loads a half-random net that logs RESUMED

finding.title: vanilla_ppo checkpoint torch.save is non-atomic and resume falls back to FRESH weights (not the previous checkpoint) when the newest file is corrupt
finding.failure_scenario: trainer.py:7391 does `torch.save(_ckpt_payload, str(ckpt_path))` straight to the final path — no tmp+fsync+rename, despite checkpointing.py's atomicity doctrine (save_checkpoint_atomic does the dance for the GA path only). Kill the process mid-save (OOM-kill, power loss, MPS crash — exactly the events the new 14010eb crash supervisor exists to absorb) and the HIGHEST-numbered vanilla_ppo_iter_*.pt is a truncated zip. On the supervisor's relaunch, _maybe_resume_vanilla_ppo (4235-4277) tries ONLY latest_ckpts[-1]; torch.load raises, the broad `except Exception` at 4273 logs 'auto-resume scan failed (starting fresh)' and returns iter_offset=0. Days of training silently restart from random weights. Worse: global_it restarts at 0, so the iter-10 save OVERWRITES the historical good vanilla_ppo_iter_00010.pt, while the corrupt high-numbered file remains the resume target forever — every subsequent crash restarts from scratch again. The supervisor turns one bad write into unbounded silent progress loss that looks like 'training is running fine'.
finding.fix_sketch: 1) Save via tmp+fsync+os.replace (reuse the exact dance from checkpointing.save_checkpoint_atomic, or add a save_torch_atomic helper there and call it for the iter checkpoint, best_cold.pt at 6536, and best_<level>.pt at 6729). 2) In _maybe_resume_vanilla_ppo, loop candidates newest→oldest: on torch.load failure, rename the bad file to *.pt.corrupt (so it stops being the resume target and never gets overwritten) and try the next-newest; only start fresh when NO checkpoint loads, and log at ERROR, not WARNING.

verdict.reasons: Every load-bearing claim checks out against the code. (1) trainer.py:7391 saves the iter checkpoint with a raw torch.save to the final path — no tmp+fsync+os.replace — while checkpointing.py's save_checkpoint_atomic explicitly does that dance for the GA file only; the payload (net + Adam state + RND + anticollapse best-net snapshot) makes the vulnerable write window seconds long every 10 iters. (4) Commit 14010eb exists (scripts/train_game.py:651-692): the supervisor auto-relaunches with auto-resume up to 5 times, making the loop fully automated and silent. Minor overstatements only: winners/ best-ever artifacts ARE saved atomically via save_winner and survive (so the deliverable isn't lost, "days of training" loss = resume/progress state and iter history, not the champion net), and "forever" is really "until numbering passes the corrupt iter". Neither changes the mechanism. Severity stays critical: silent, compounding loss of multi-day training progress plus destruction of good historical checkpoints, in a system whose new supervisor is specifically designed to relaunch unattended.

finding.title: Consolidation gate accepts/`DONE`s the deliverable with zero protect-level evidence when protect probes fail — and reports protect_min=1.0 while doing it

Outcome: a weld that catastrophically forgot 1-1 gets pinned as the accepted champion and the campaign builds on it.
finding.fix_sketch: Track probe failures explicitly: n_protect_failed = number of entries where _pr is None. Gate accept AND done on `n_protect_failed == 0` (hold otherwise); after N consecutive probe-failure iters, log.error and pause/abort the consolidation mode instead of training blind. Emit consolidate_protect_min as NaN/None (or -1) when no protect probe succeeded, never 1.0, and emit a consolidate_probe_failures counter.

(1) cold_probe.py:294-317 catches timeout/non-zero-exit/JSON-error/any-Exception and returns _base_result with cold_seq_clear_rate=None — probe failures are indistinguishable from missing data. (5) gate_step (oneshot_curriculum.py:350-354) with regressed=None will ACCEPT (best_<level>.pt written, trainer.py:6721-6746) and reach DONE (marker written that chains the next level, 6766-6800). finding.title: Go-Explore archive: non-atomic pickle save + swallowed load failure means a crash mid-save silently zeroes the archive, then the empty archive overwrites the recoverable file

finding.title: save_winner compares metric_value across DIFFERENT metric_names, so a stale (historically inflated) clear_rate winner silently blocks the honest cold-sequential champion forever

The same per-game winners/ slot is written with metric_name='clear_rate' by default mode (trainer.py:7423-7429) and 'cold_seq_clear_rate' by ladder mode (7413-7421). The comparison of incomparable metrics corrupts winner promotion in whichever direction the numbers happen to fall.

verdict.reasons: Every link of the claimed failure path checks out in code. (1) save_winner (checkpointing.py:350-357) compares only prev metric_value against the new value and never compares metric_name — repo-wide grep shows metric_name is write-only. (2) The refusal is silent: bare `return False` at line 357, log only on success (line 403), and both trainer.py call sites (7414, 7423) discard the return value. (3) The same per-game winners/ slot (checkpoints/<slug>/winners/, via derive_checkpoint_dir in profile_utils.py:56-75) is written with metric_name="cold_seq_clear_rate" in ladder mode (trainer.py:7412-7421) and "clear_rate" in default mode (7422-7430). Severity stays medium: the cold champion's weights are independently persisted as best_cold.pt (trainer.py:6535-6542), so there is no data loss or training corruption — the impact is silent wrong-artifact selection on the make demo/make eval path, contingent on a cross-metric-regime history in the same per-game checkpoint dir (exactly the current SMB campaign situation). finding.title: Torn vanilla_ppo checkpoint is a permanent poison pill: non-atomic torch.save + newest-only resume with catch-all silently restarts training from random weights
finding.failure_scenario: trainer.py:7391 writes the vanilla_ppo checkpoint with a direct `torch.save(_ckpt_payload, str(ckpt_path))` — no tmp+rename, even though the atomic helper exists unused for this path (checkpointing.py:56-91). The payload (net + optimizer + RND + anticollapse best_net_snapshot) is hundreds of MB, so the write window is seconds. The new crash supervisor (train_game.py:662-690, shipped 14010eb) guarantees this path is exercised: OOM-kill/SIGKILL/power-loss mid-save leaves a truncated vanilla_ppo_iter_01230.pt. On relaunch, _maybe_resume_vanilla_ppo picks ONLY the newest by iter number (trainer.py:4236-4241), torch.load raises, and the blanket `except` at 4273-4277 logs a WARNING and 'starts fresh' — it never tries the older good checkpoints sitting in the same dir. Worse, the fresh run restarts numbering at 0, so no future save ever outnumbers the torn file: every subsequent crash/resume hits the same torn newest and silently retrains from random weights forever. Same class: go_explore archive.pkl is also written non-atomically (go_explore.py:255-256); a torn archive is caught at trainer.py:5199 and silently replaced with an EMPTY archive, discarding days of frontier memory. tests/test_resume_roundtrip.py:87 is happy-path only — no torn-file case exists anywhere in tests/.

Effort: ~2h fix + 2h tests. Add both to a `make gauntlet` target = test-fast + this file + test_resume_roundtrip + test_auto_reset_on_death + test_sticky_actions + parity smoke (~30min of Makefile work).

verdict.reasons: Every cited code path checks out. (1) trainer.py:7391 writes the vanilla_ppo checkpoint via bare torch.save to the final path — no tmp+rename — while checkpointing.py:56-91 provides save_checkpoint_atomic whose docstring explicitly promises the mid-write-kill guarantee this path violates; the atomic helper is used only for GA gen_*.pt (trainer.py:7449). (2) _maybe_resume_vanilla_ppo (trainer.py:4236-4241) loads ONLY the highest-numbered checkpoint; the blanket except at 4273-4277 logs a WARNING and returns iter_offset=0 — no fallback to older good checkpoints in the same dir. (3) global_it = it + iter_offset (trainer.py:5263), so a failed resume restarts numbering at 0: subsequent saves cannot outnumber the torn file, and additionally OVERWRITE the old run's good low-numbered checkpoints at the same filenames (a clobber hazard test_resume_roundtrip.py:143-148 itself documents). rotate_old_checkpoints globs only gen_*.pt (checkpointing.py:154-156), so the torn file is never evicted. (5) go_explore.py:255-256 non-atomic pickle confirmed; torn archive caught at trainer.py:5199-5200, run continues with the empty archive from 5187, and the periodic save at 7437-7441 overwrites archive.pkl with it. (6) No torn/corrupt-checkpoint test exists anywhere in tests/ — all grep hits are unrelated contexts; test_resume_roundtrip.py:87 is happy-path only. Severity corrected critical→high: the mechanism fires exactly as described and the consequence (silent, self-perpetuating loss of multi-day training progress at WARNING log level) is maximal, but the trigger requires a kill landing inside the save window or persistent disk-full — an edge condition, and the current SMB campaign's tile mode has a ~few-MB payload (14k-param MLP) with a millisecond window, not the 'hundreds of MB / seconds' claimed (that applies to pixel-CNN games). finding.title: Five Mario profiles alias the same checkpoint dir, and auto-resume (default ON) silently resumes a different recipe's checkpoint

A downloader trains with `make train GAME=mario` (mario_vanilla_ppo), then explores configs/ and re-launches with `--profile configs/mario_tiles.yaml`: --resume defaults to True (scripts/train_game.py:504), the vanilla_ppo_iter_*.pt scan (src/training/trainer.py:4224) finds the OTHER recipe's checkpoint, and if architectures happen to match, training silently continues a foreign lineage while run_manifest.json is overwritten with the new profile — provenance and every subsequent eval/metric are attributed to the wrong recipe (same silent-invalidation class as the dead --start-state incident). If architectures mismatch, startup raises, and the new crash supervisor (scripts/train_game.py:662-694) relaunches with auto-resume into the same mismatched checkpoint 5 times (60s backoff each, ~5 min of futile restarts) before aborting. eval_game.py:210 derives the identical dir, so `make eval GAME=mario` also scores whichever profile trained last.

The manifest already stores the profile (train_game.py:626-638), so the hook exists. Also have the supervisor detect a resume-time architecture error as non-retryable (fail fast, don't burn the 5-restart budget).

verdict.reasons: Core defect verified end-to-end. (1) derive_checkpoint_dir (src/training/profile_utils.py:75) slugs only the profile's display `name`, and all five mario configs declare name: "Super Mario Bros." — verified by grep — so mario.yaml, mario_canonical.yaml, mario_tiles.yaml, mario_vanilla_shaped.yaml, and mario_vanilla_ppo.yaml all alias checkpoints/super_mario_bros/ (applied at trainer.py:190 with the default base; launcher passes no override). (2) --resume defaults True (scripts/train_game.py:504) and make train GAME=mario resolves to mario_vanilla_ppo.yaml. (3) The silent foreign-lineage resume genuinely fires: mario_vanilla_ppo and mario_vanilla_shaped are architecturally identical (7 actions, smb_tiles encoder, tile_frame_stack 4, both trainer_mode vanilla_ppo), so _maybe_resume_vanilla_ppo (trainer.py:4237-4272) loads the other recipe's vanilla_ppo_iter_*.pt with only a log line naming a file path that carries no profile identity. (4) run_manifest.json is unconditionally overwritten with the new profile (write_run_manifest atomic-replaces; NO code reads it back as a guard — verified by grep), so provenance misattributes the lineage. (5) eval_game.py:210 derives the identical dir, so make eval scores whichever profile trained last. HOWEVER, two branches of the narrative are wrong, which is why severity drops to medium: (a) the crash-supervisor 5×60s restart-loop branch is REFUTED — the entire resume load sits inside try/except Exception (trainer.py:4235-4277) that logs "auto-resume scan failed (starting fresh)" and continues; an architecture-mismatch RuntimeError never escapes to the supervisor; (b) the finding's chosen example pair (relaunch with mario_tiles.yaml) does not fire the silent path: mario_tiles is trainer_mode ga_ppo, which never reaches the vanilla_ppo scan (gate at trainer.py:1484), and its 6-action head mismatches the 7-action checkpoint anyway — that pair only cross-contaminates shared dir artifacts (manifest, curriculum states). Additional unclaimed mitigation: _archive_previous_run (trainer.py:1375) snapshots the prior run's metrics + profile YAML into runs/<ts>/ at each start, so the corruption is silent at run time but forensically recoverable. Net: the headline silent-invalidation fires with default flags between the two most-likely-swapped shipped recipes (vanilla_ppo ↔ vanilla_shaped) and corrupts provenance/eval attribution — real and worth fixing (the fix_sketch's manifest-comparison guard is sound; note the manifest stores trainer_mode/encoder/hyperparams, not a profile path/hash) — but the crash-loop amplifier is fabricated and the silent-resume blast radius is one config pair, not all five.

finding.title: Every line in run.log is written twice in two different formats; raw Rust stderr (panics, pool prints) is only captured by accident
finding.failure_scenario: Confirmed in every shipped log (e.g. checkpoints/mario_1_1_sticky_calibration/run.log, checkpoints/mario_2_1_runB/run.log): each record appears once as "22:33:46 [INFO] ..." (the stderr basicConfig format, scripts/train_game.py:590-594) and again as "2026-07-19 22:33:46,974 INFO ..." (the root FileHandler format, trainer.py:1134-1136), because the standard headless launch redirects stderr into the same <checkpoint_dir>/run.log the FileHandler opens — the un-prefixed "[nes_core::Pool] start state ..." line in the log proves fd 2 points at run.log. Consequences: log volume doubles, the docstring's own contract ("keep the format stable so downstream log parsing doesn't break", src/utils/logging_config.py:9) is broken, and grep/parse tooling sees every event twice. Worse, if a user redirects with `>` (truncate) instead of `>>`, the 'w'-mode truncation at trainer.py:1119 desyncs the two independent fd offsets and the log gets NUL-hole corrupted. And when the user does NOT redirect, Rust-side panics/aborts — the exact evidence needed for the panic_isolation=OFF crash class — never reach run.log at all, since they bypass Python logging.
finding.fix_sketch: In _attach_run_file_logger, os.fstat(2) and compare (st_dev, st_ino) with run_log's stat: if stderr already IS run.log, skip attaching the FileHandler (stderr formatting wins). Better: make the launcher own forensics — train_game.py os.dup2()s stdout/stderr into <checkpoint_dir>/run.log (append mode) before building the Trainer and the FileHandler is dropped entirely; that also captures Rust panics, abort() messages, and MPS driver spew, which the current design misses.

verdict.reasons: Empirically confirmed in both cited logs: checkpoints/mario_2_1_runB/run.log contains exactly 353 lines = 176 stderr-basicConfig-format ("14:03:56 [INFO] ...", from scripts/train_game.py:590-594) + 176 FileHandler-format ("2026-07-18 14:03:56,273 INFO ...", from trainer.py:1132-1136) + 1 raw un-prefixed "[nes_core::Pool] start state ..." line; mario_1_1_sticky_calibration/run.log shows the identical pattern. The raw Rust line proves fd 2 was shell-redirected into the same run.log the root FileHandler appends to, so every Python logging record is written twice in two formats, breaking the stated parsing contract at src/utils/logging_config.py:9. The "Rust stderr captured only by accident" claim is also confirmed: the FileHandler receives only Python logging records, so without the shell redirect, Rust panics (the exact panic_isolation=OFF crash class these logs warn about) never reach run.log. Two caveats: (1) the NUL-hole corruption scenario under `>` redirection is mechanically valid POSIX behavior against the 'w'-mode truncate at trainer.py:1119, but is unrealized — both shipped logs contain 0 NUL bytes (user launches with append-mode redirect); (2) duplication is contingent on the user's redirect practice, though both shipped logs prove that practice is the standard launch. Severity corrected to medium: real contract violation, 2x log volume, and missing crash forensics, but no impact on training artifacts, checkpoints, or metrics, and the log remains usable — "high" overstates a log-hygiene defect.

finding.title: Supervisor relaunch treats a crash-continuation as a brand-new run: truncates run.log and fragments/erases mid-incident forensics
finding.failure_scenario: On each supervised relaunch, trainer.run() unconditionally re-runs _archive_previous_run() + metrics truncate + _attach_run_file_logger() (src/training/trainer.py:1375-1383). Fast-fail case (the poisoned-checkpoint class the supervisor was built for, one day old and unreviewed): the crash happens before the first metrics row, so archive_previous_run no-ops on the empty metrics file (src/training/checkpointing.py:210-211) — run.log is then truncated by open(run_log, "w") at trainer.py:1119, destroying the traceback the supervisor just logged. Attempts 1..4's tracebacks are erased one by one; after "restart budget exhausted" only the final attempt's traceback survives, so a mixed-cause crash loop (transient MPS error then poison save) is un-diagnosable — a repeat of the '2h dead, no forensics' incident shape. Slow-crash case: metrics.jsonl is shutil.move'd into runs/<ts>/ (checkpointing.py:217) on every relaunch, so one supervised session shatters its metrics timeline across N archive dirs and the GUI dashboard/scoreboard watching checkpoints/<slug>/metrics.jsonl sees progress reset to zero after every auto-heal.
finding.fix_sketch: Thread a relaunch flag from the supervisor into run() (e.g. trainer.run(..., relaunch=attempt>0)) that skips _archive_previous_run/_metrics_sink.truncate and opens run.log in append mode; alternatively have the supervisor write every crash traceback to its own append-only <checkpoint_dir>/supervisor.log before calling run(), and make _attach_run_file_logger append (mode 'a') whenever metrics were not archived.

verdict.reasons: Every link in the claimed chain checks out in code. (1) The supervisor loop (scripts/train_game.py:662-694) re-invokes trainer.run() on each relaunch with no relaunch flag; run() unconditionally executes _archive_previous_run() + _metrics_sink.truncate() + _attach_run_file_logger() (src/training/trainer.py:1375-1383). (2) Fast-fail case confirmed exactly: MetricsSink.truncate() leaves metrics.jsonl at size 0 (metrics_sink.py:89), so a crash before the first metrics row makes archive_previous_run() return None (checkpointing.py:210-211) — run.log is preserved only via that archive path, and open(run_log, "w") at trainer.py:1119 then destroys it. (3) The traceback genuinely is in run.log when truncated: the FileHandler is on the root logger and is detached only at the start of the NEXT _attach_run_file_logger call (trainer.py:1124-1131); _teardown() (trainer.py:7539-7572) never touches handlers, so the supervisor's log.error traceback lands in run.log and the next relaunch erases it — in a fast-fail loop only the final attempt's traceback survives on disk. (4) Slow-crash fragmentation confirmed: shutil.move (checkpointing.py:217) scatters one supervised session's metrics across N runs/<ts>/ dirs, and checkpoints/<slug>/metrics.jsonl is watched by src/gui/training_dashboard.py and scripts/scoreboard.py, which see a reset. Severity corrected high → medium: the slow-crash half is fragmentation, not erasure (run.log incl. traceback is copy2'd into the archive before truncation, metrics are moved not deleted, recoverable by concatenating runs/*/); all tracebacks also hit stderr via basicConfig (irretrievable only when stderr isn't captured, e.g. headless/GUI launches); the final budget-exhausting traceback always survives; and no checkpoints, training progress, or auto-resume behavior are harmed. It is a real forensics/observability defect in the supervisor's core purpose, but not data/progress loss. Fix sketch is sound: thread relaunch=attempt>0 into run() to skip archive/truncate and append to run.log, or have the supervisor append each traceback to its own supervisor.log before relaunching.

finding.title: setup-check reports '[nes_core] import OK' with zero build provenance — the documented maturin-stale-.so failure mode is undetectable
finding.failure_scenario: This project has a memory-documented recurring trap: `make build` (Makefile:86, maturin develop) can leave the venv's nes_core.abi3.so stale, so Python keeps running the OLD engine after a Rust fix. Neither setup-check (train_game.py:351-356 prints only 'import OK'), the launcher banner, nor the run manifest records which nes_core build is actually loaded — python.rs exposes no __version__/git-SHA/build-timestamp at all. Concrete scenario: a downloader pulls a rewards.rs fix (e.g. the World-2 reward-desert fix, 935e609), runs `make build`, sees success, retrains overnight — and trains 8 hours on the pre-fix engine with every surface (setup-check, run.log, run_manifest.json) claiming a healthy environment. This is the Rust-side twin of the sticky_action_prob dead-knob class: the fix exists, is 'installed', and never executes.
finding.fix_sketch: Embed provenance in the extension via build.rs (git describe + build UTC timestamp) and expose nes_core.build_info(); print it in run_setup_check and the [launcher] banner, and store it in run_manifest.json. In the Makefile build target, hash .venv/**/nes_core.abi3.so before and after maturin and fail loudly with the known-workaround message (cp target/release/libnes_core.dylib -> venv .so) if unchanged while sources are newer. setup-check should additionally warn when the .so mtime predates the newest nes_core/src/*.rs mtime.

verdict.reasons: Every claim traced and verified. (1) train_game.py:351-356: setup-check prints only '[nes_core] import OK (rom_info=...)' — zero build provenance. (2) nes_core/src/python.rs pymodule (lines 1234-1257) exports only classes/functions/button constants; no __version__, no build_info(), and no build.rs exists. (3) Makefile:86 'build' is a bare 'maturin develop --release' with no dylib post-copy or before/after .so hash check, despite the project's own memory (project_maturin_stale_install) documenting that the venv nes_core.abi3.so must be manually copied after every make build or Python runs the old engine. (4) src/training/run_manifest.py records git_commit of the source tree — in the stale-.so scenario the manifest would affirmatively attest the FIXED commit while the pre-fix engine ran, which is worse than the finding states. (5) Launcher '[launcher]' banner logs only profile/ROM/checkpoint paths. (6) Grep for abi3/dylib/stale across Makefile, scripts/, src/training/ finds no staleness guard anywhere; package version is pinned 0.1.0 in Cargo.toml/pyproject.toml so dist-info metadata cannot distinguish builds either. The scenario genuinely fires: the stale-install trap is memory-documented as recurring in this environment, and all health surfaces report OK (manifest reports wrong provenance) during a wasted overnight run. Severity medium is correct: it is a missing guard/observability gap, not an active defect, and the primary user knows the manual workaround — but the consequence class (silently invalidated multi-hour training runs plus falsified provenance in the reproducibility manifest) is too costly for low.

finding.title: make setup-check — the tool that diagnoses a broken environment — dies with a cryptic shell error when the environment is broken (missing/half-built .venv)
finding.failure_scenario: Every Makefile target, including setup-check itself, starts with `. .venv/bin/activate &&`. A fresh-clone user who runs `make setup-check` before (or after a mid-way-aborted) scripts/install_macos.sh gets `sh: .venv/bin/activate: No such file or directory` + `make: *** [setup-check] Error 1` — no mention of the installer, no next step, from the very command README ("Run `make setup-check` first") positions as the environment doctor whose own docstring promises to be "deliberately crash-proof ... the whole point is to tell a fresh clone what's still needed" (train_game.py:341-343). Same cryptic wall for `make train`/`make gui` when a Python upgrade breaks the venv symlinks. Note the repo already knows the better pattern — provenance-check (Makefile:137) invokes .venv/bin/python directly.
finding.fix_sketch: Add a guard prerequisite used by all venv-dependent targets: `venv-guard:\n\t@test -x .venv/bin/python || { echo 'No .venv found — run: bash scripts/install_macos.sh (see README Install)'; exit 1; }` and switch targets to invoke `.venv/bin/python` directly instead of sourcing activate. Then `make setup-check` on a broken venv prints one actionable line instead of a shell error.

verdict.reasons: Reproduced end-to-end: copied the Makefile to a scratch dir with no .venv and ran `make setup-check` — output is exactly `/bin/sh: .venv/bin/activate: No such file or directory` + `make: *** [setup-check] Error 1` (exit 2), with no pointer to scripts/install_macos.sh. Makefile:50 matches the citation, and every Python-facing target (train, eval, gui, test, ...) shares the same `. .venv/bin/activate &&` prefix. The self-contradiction claim verifies verbatim: run_setup_check() in scripts/train_game.py documents itself as "Deliberately crash-proof ... the whole point is to tell a fresh clone what's still needed" and even prints a friendly hint for the venv-not-active case — but the Makefile wrapper crashes before the function can run in exactly that case. README line 94 positions `make setup-check` as the first command ("Run `make setup-check` first — it verifies your environment (venv, ...)"), and Makefile:137 (provenance-check) confirms the repo already uses the better direct `.venv/bin/python` pattern. Minor overstatements that don't change the verdict: (a) "Every Makefile target" — build/clean/provenance-check/ppu_layout_check don't source activate, but all venv-dependent ones do including setup-check itself; (b) the README's Install section does order install_macos.sh before setup-check, so a strictly sequential reader installs first — but skimmers, aborted installs, and Python-upgrade-broken venvs still hit the wall, which is the doctor command's target audience. Severity medium is correct for a ux-polish finding: no data corruption or wrong results, but the flagship first-run onboarding command fails with a bare shell error in the exact scenario it exists to diagnose, which matters given the project's active customer-onboarding program.
